lesson.title: Worry Without an Off Switch: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
lesson.summary: Generalized anxiety disorder is excessive, hard-to-control worry that spreads across many areas of life rather than attaching to one specific trigger, keeping the body's stress response chronically engaged.
lesson.body:
Generalized anxiety disorder is defined by excessive anxiety and worry, occurring more days than not for at least six months, about a number of different events or activities rather than any single concern. Crucially, the worry is difficult for the person to control: they cannot simply decide to stop thinking about it or reassure themselves out of it. The diagnosis also requires at least three of the following (only one is required in children): restlessness or feeling keyed up, being easily fatigued, difficulty concentrating or the mind going blank, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance. Together, these criteria describe a pattern less like fear pointed at a specific object and more like a general, free-floating state of apprehension that attaches itself to whatever is currently uncertain in a person's life: work performance one day, a family member's health the next, finances after that.

This pattern connects directly to what is known about stress and behavior. The body's stress response is built to handle discrete, resolvable threats: it activates, the person deals with the situation, and the response winds back down. Generalized anxiety disorder disrupts that wind-down process. Because the worry is not tied to one identifiable, resolvable problem, but instead migrates from concern to concern, the physiological stress response has no clear endpoint and stays engaged for extended periods. Muscle tension, fatigue, and disrupted sleep are not incidental symptoms here, they are what a chronically activated stress response looks like when it never fully switches off, and that ongoing physical strain can, in turn, make it even harder to think clearly or feel calm, feeding the worry further.

Picture someone who wakes up already anticipating problems: whether a work project will go badly, whether a minor ache means something serious, whether they said the wrong thing in a conversation days ago, whether their finances will hold up. No single one of these worries would necessarily be unusual on its own, but the person cannot set any of them down, and as soon as one resolves, another takes its place. That inability to localize the anxiety to one specific trigger, and the constant background hum of tension it produces, is what distinguishes generalized anxiety disorder from something like a specific phobia, where the fear at least has a clear, identifiable target.
